title: Dentate Granule Cells
intro: Dentate granule cells are small excitatory neurons packed by the million into the dentate gyrus, the hippocampus's input stage. They are among the quietest neurons in the brain: only a few per cent are active in any environment, and they are hard to excite because they rest far below threshold and are wrapped in strong inhibition. That sparseness is thought to be the point: the dentate gyrus spreads similar entorhinal inputs into very different, barely overlapping codes, so that CA3 can store them without interference.

items: Numbers: about one million granule cells per hemisphere in rat, versus about 200,000 entorhinal layer 2 input cells and about 250,000 CA3 cells (Amaral et al. 1990). The entorhinal-to-dentate step is an expansion, much like the projection-neuron-to-Kenyon-cell step in the insect mushroom body (see Mushroom Bodies, #/neuroscience/mushroom-bodies).

Morphology: a small oval soma in the granule cell layer, a cone of spiny dendrites in the molecular layer (with no basal dendrites in mature cells), and an unmyelinated axon, the mossy fibre, that makes a few large boutons on CA3 pyramidal cells and many small contacts on interneurons and mossy cells in the hilus.

Intrinsic properties: very hyperpolarised resting potential (about −75 to −85 mV), low input resistance in mature cells, strong spike-frequency adaptation; dendrites strongly attenuate distal input (Krueppel, Remy & Beck 2011).

Activity: sparse. In a given environment only around 1 to 5 per cent of granule cells fire, typically with one or a few small place fields (Chawla et al. 2005; GoodSmith et al. 2017; Diamantaki et al. 2016).
Inhibition: strong feedforward and feedback inhibition from basket cells and other dentate interneurons, plus excitation and inhibition through hilar mossy cells.

Adult neurogenesis: in rodents new granule cells are born throughout life. For a few weeks after birth they are more excitable and more plastic than mature cells (Schmidt-Hieber, Jonas & Bischofberger 2004; Ge et al. 2007), and they are thought to help separate new memories. Whether adult neurogenesis continues at a meaningful rate in humans is debated (Sorrells et al. 2018 against; Moreno-Jimenez et al. 2019 for).

blocks.text: Pattern separation means turning similar inputs into less similar outputs. A sparse expansion code does this naturally: when each granule cell needs several coincident inputs to fire and inhibition lets only the most strongly driven cells through, a small change in the input set changes which cells cross threshold. Leutgeb et al. (2007) showed this in rats: small changes to the shape of an enclosure substantially changed which dentate granule cells fired, while CA3 responded more in an all-or-none way. Mice lacking NMDA receptors in granule cells struggle to tell similar contexts apart (McHugh et al. 2007).

items: Santhakumar, Aradi and Soltesz (2005): a widely used dentate gyrus network model with multi-compartment granule cells, mossy cells, basket cells and HIPP cells, built to study epilepsy-related sprouting; Dyhrfjeld-Johnsen et al. (2007) scaled it to a full-size 1:1 network.

Aradi and Holmes (1999) and Schmidt-Hieber, Jonas and Bischofberger (2007): detailed compartmental granule cell models; Beining et al. (2017) built a large set of granule cell models with realistic morphologies and ion channel distributions (T2N toolbox).

Myers and Scharfman (2009) and Chavlis, Petrantonakis and Poirazi (2017): network models of pattern separation in which granule cell sparseness and dendritic properties determine how much input overlap is reduced.
Neurogenesis models: Aimone, Wiles and Gage (2009) and others model new, more excitable granule cells joining a network and show how they could separate memories formed at different times.
Abstract models: random expansion plus k-winners-take-all inhibition (as in Marr 1971 and Treves-Rolls 1994) captures pattern separation with very simple units.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: To separate similar inputs, use a large expansion layer with sparse, random input connections, a high threshold and strong inhibition (k-WTA), and keep only 1 to 5 per cent of cells active.
The same design appears in the cerebellar granule layer and the mushroom body, and in the spatial pooler of HTM: it is one of biology's most reused tricks.
Strong mossy-fibre-like 'detonator' synapses from the expansion layer to a recurrent memory layer let one sparse pattern impose itself during learning.
